findings.title: Conditional will and source control
findings.claim: The focus makes withdrawal a possibility within divine will; 13:39 also couples what God wills with erasure and establishment, while 76:30 places human willing within God's will. Together the wider lines make the conditional an agency boundary: the revelation may be received, but its retention does not become the recipient's power.
findings.mechanism: The focus's ordinary willing verb introduces a hypothetical whose result is taking away what was revealed. The supplied 13:39 surface pairs erasing and establishing with God's willing, and 76:30 places human willing within God's. These contacts return through the focus's will and removal predicates, making the conditional a wider relation of agency without turning it into an announced outcome.
findings.reader_payoff: The conditional can be read as a boundary on control rather than a forecast: the addressee receives revelation within a will that also governs erasure and establishment.
findings.containment: Nothing says the revelation is in fact taken away here. The wider verses do not identify a lost object or specify a mechanism, so they deepen the focus's conditional without replacing it.

epistemic.reason: The initiating reader-walk support is legacy_unbound. The focus bridge is complete and both target Arabic surfaces are supplied, but the 13:39 row is a reciprocal nomination and target morphology is absent.

findings.title: Received revelation under source authority
findings.claim: The focus makes what was revealed the object of possible removal. Cross-surah passages pair that possibility with a human request to change the Quran, which the messenger cannot do on his own, with divine replacement, with recitation of the revealed words, and with God's guarding of the Reminder. The relation presents revelation as received communication whose alteration and keeping remain with its source.
findings.mechanism: The focus's removal verb carries movement away from the addressee, and its object is the communication sent to him. In 10:15 a demand for another Quran or a change is answered by following what is revealed; 16:101 places substitution with divine sending; 18:27 joins recitation to words that have no changer; and 15:9 names God as the one who sent down and guards the Reminder. These contacts turn possible removal from an image of recipient-held property into a boundary on who can alter, preserve, or withdraw the message.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees a receiver who can recite and follow a message while its alteration and keeping remain source-governed; the hypothetical removal does not grant the receiver control over it.
findings.containment: The focus states a possibility, not an actual removal. God's guarding in 15:9 remains alongside the conditional, and divine replacement in 16:101 is not equated with the focus's taking-away.

epistemic.reason: The reader-walk source is legacy_unbound. Focus carriers and exact target Arabic are supplied, but the connection rows are nominations without target morphology, and the retained synthesis is interpretive.

findings.title: The direction of the wakil
findings.claim: The focus seeks a wakil for the addressee in relation to God, while other verses direct reliance toward God as wakil and call Him sufficient in that role. The role is present in both places, but its direction changes: no delegate stands against God, while reliance is toward Him.
findings.mechanism: The focus's phrase places the searched-for wakil on the addressee's side and against the divine speaker. In 33:3 Allah is the sufficient wakil, and 73:9 says to take Him as wakil; 6:102 extends that role over everything. The shared role term meets opposing participant directions and turns the final failed search into a boundary on advocacy rather than a general absence of care.
findings.reader_payoff: The final inability concerns an advocate against God; beside it, the wider verses leave reliance on God as wakil fully visible.
findings.containment: The wider verses do not turn 17:86 into a direct command to rely on God or identify a wakil for this specific removal. The focus retains its conditional and its denial of an advocate against God.

epistemic.reason: The focus branch and QAC occurrence are supplied, and exact target Arabic is present. The connection rows nominate the relation but do not supply target morphology or a trust label.

findings.title: Removal and remembered recitation
findings.claim: A cross-surah echo lets the focus's possible taking-away touch remembered and recited access as well as the presence of a message: 87:6-7 ties the messenger's recitation, forgetting, and an exception of God's will together.
findings.mechanism: The focus's transitive removal verb carries departure of what was revealed. The supplied 87:6-7 surfaces describe God causing the messenger to recite so he does not forget, with an exception tied to divine will; that contact makes continued recitation and memory one possible dimension of what taking-away could affect.
findings.reader_payoff: The possible loss can be pictured as an interruption of recited or remembered access as well as removal of a message-object, while the exact mode remains open.
findings.containment: The focus does not specify forgetting as its mode of removal, and 87:6-7 does not establish that anything is withdrawn in 17:86. This remains an exploratory echo, not a lexical gloss.

epistemic.reason: The focus carrier and both target Arabic surfaces are supplied, but the mode-of-removal contact is interpretive and target morphology is absent.
